sections.explanation: For a positive integer n, aⁿ means n factors of a multiplied together. It is not a×n. Multiplying powers with the same base joins the factors: aᵐaⁿ=aᵐ⁺ⁿ. Dividing cancels factors: aᵐ/aⁿ=aᵐ⁻ⁿ when a≠0. Consistency with a/a=1 gives a⁰=1 for a≠0; a negative exponent denotes a reciprocal, a⁻ⁿ=1/aⁿ. Zero to a negative power is undefined. We do not assign a value to 0⁰ here. A power of a product distributes across factors; a power of a sum generally does not.

sections.explanation: The principal square root √x is the non-negative number whose square is x; it is real only for x≥0. Thus√9=3, although the equation y²=9 has two solutions,3 and −3. Odd roots can be negative: the real cube root of −8 is −2. For positive a, define aᵖ⁄ᑫ as the qth root of aᵖ; positive-base exponent laws remain consistent. At zero, negative powers are excluded. Negative bases with fractional exponents require careful domain choices; do not apply all positive-base exponent rules to them without justification. In this lesson use positive bases for rational-power manipulation, and discuss negative numbers only through explicit odd roots.

sections.explanation: Python writes powers with **. Exponentiation binds more tightly than unary minus, so -3**2 gives −9; (-3)**2 gives 9. An import makes a library available: import math lets you call math.sqrt(...). The dot selects a function provided by that library; you are using a supplied function, not yet defining your own. math.sqrt expects a non-negative real input. A ValueError indicates an unacceptable value for that operation. Do not treat a fractional power of a negative base in Python as a general real odd-root calculator.
